messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] linear regression: infer points (mean, sd) instead of slopes
parts:
You need a model for the missingness. See the chapter on missing data
in the Stan manual. In a typical Bayesian setting, you create a joint
model p(y, x, beta) and then turn the usual Bayesian crank to draw
from p(x | y, beta) just as you would draw from p(beta | x, y).
That is, declare y and beta as data and x as a parameter, code the
joint density in Stan and push the button.

- Bob

unconstrained and not used.

I'm afraid I don't follow why you are running
log_sum_exp. What is comb[p]?

If it's a mixture model at some level, you can
have problems with identifiability.

For efficiency, you don't want to have to keep applying
log(a[s, p]) --- you can do it once in transformed data
to define a variable log_a where log_a[s, p] = log(a[s, p]).

Not sure why you're then considering normal_lcdf.

What's the model trying to do?

parts:
Sorry for the confusion, trying to simplify my model as example was not the best idea.

#1 Let's take stan manual example for linear regression (alpha = 0, beta_1 and beta_2)

--------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] x_1;
vector[N] x_2;
vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
real beta_1;
real beta_2;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
y ~ normal(beta_1 * x_1 + beta_2 * x_2, sigma);
}
--------------------------------

#2 let's suppose I have many beta as data and one x as parameter. The model becomes

--------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] beta_1;
vector[N] beta_2;
vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
real x_1;
real x_2;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
y ~ normal(beta_1 * x_1 + beta_2 * x_2, sigma);
}

everything comes about: parameters beta and sigma

If y and phi are both known, then it gets tricky. You
only have two degrees of freedom, and given that the theta

0 < theta[n, 1] * phi[n, 1] < y[n]

0 < theta[n, 2] * phi[n, 2] < y[n] - theta[n, 1] * phi[n, 1]

theta3[n] = y[n] - (theta1[n] * phi[n, 1]) + (theta2[n] * phi[n, 2]);

You have to do those two constraints custom, define theta3 as

Why do you want mean(theta) and sd(theta)? If they come from
a hierarchical normal prior, why not use its mean and standard deviation?

If you really just want those quantities, Stan has functions mean(theta)
and sd(theta) for sample means and standard deviations. So you can define
those as transformed parameters or generated quantities. But I wouldn't
try to put a distribution on them as it will no longer be a clean generative
model. And if you do insist on putting a distribution on them, then you
need to take care of the Jacobian adjustment manually by incrementing the
target log density.
